## Methods

Strains
Leuconostoc mesenteroides C7M43 (LM), Leuconostoc citreum 4367 (LC4), Leuconostoc citreum 200443 (LC2), Lactococcus lactis CCFM 1092 (A01), Lactococcus lactis CCFM 1032 (B01), and Enterobacter hormaechei 42D12 (EH1) were laboratory-preserved strains sourced from natural isolates from fermented chilies. In the previous work36, it was found that strains LM, A01, and B01 occupied the niche in fermented chiles for the first 4 days with a relative abundance of more than 1%. Strain LM is commonly used as a starter in fermented foods due to its ability to acidify the substrate rapidly. Strains A01 and B01 are producers of good flavor. Strain EH1 is a common spoilage bacterium in fermented foods that can easily invade foods and cause spoilage. They interact with each other in the pre-fermentation stage, leading to the normalization of fermented foods. Therefore, we chose LM as the producer, A01 and B01 as the competitors, and EH1 as the invader, which differ from each other in growth rate and acid tolerance as shown in Fig. S11, Fig. S12, and Table S2.

Other environmentally selected strains, including Lactococcus lactis JGB19 (LJ9), Saccharomyces cerevisiae Y2-7 (SY2-7), Saccharomyces cerevisiae JGF28 (SJ28), and Saccharomyces cerevisiae XZFM13-1 (SX131), used to validate acid-induced cross-feeding, were laboratory-preserved strains derived from natural isolates from the gut. The other strains used to test the lactate inhibition effect (Fig. 2C) were randomly selected from a library of laboratory-preserved strains. The detailed characterization of the strains is shown in Table S2.

Growth media
De Man Rogosa-Sharpe (MRS) liquid medium and preparation of MRS agar plate. MRS liquid medium was made as described by Liao et al.36. MRS agar plates were prepared by autoclaving a mixture of MRS liquid medium and 1.5% (w/v) agar. The temperature of the sterilized mixture was maintained above 50°C to prevent the agar from solidifying. Fifteen mL of the mixture was added to a petri dish (Sorfa, 100mm×15mm). Following solidification of the agar, the plates were stored at 4°C. Antibiotics were added, if required, at the following final concentrations: erythromycin (Em; 200ng mL−1) and chloramphenicol (Cm; 25µg mL−1).

Chemically defined medium (CDM)
CDM liquid medium was made as described by Olga et al.49. CDMG liquid medium was 2% glucose added to CDM liquid medium, and CDMS liquid medium was 2% sucrose added to CDM liquid medium. CDMG or CDMS agar plates were prepared in the same way as MRS agar plates, except that CDMG or CDMS liquid medium was mixed with 1.0% (w/v) agar.

Luria-Bertani (LB) medium
The components of the LB liquid medium contain peptone 10g L−1, yeast extract powder 5g L−1, and NaCl 10g L−1. LB agar plates were prepared in the same way as MRS agar plates, except that LB liquid medium was mixed with 1.5% (w/v) agar. Antibiotics were added, if required, at the following final concentrations: erythromycin (Em; 200ng mL−1) and chloramphenicol (Cm; 25µg mL−1).

Strongly buffered MOPS medium
We prepared a strongly buffered medium by mixing 3-(N-morpholino)propanesulfonic acid (MOPS) buffer with CDMG liquid medium, in which the final concentration of MOPS was 100 mM. Strongly buffered agar plates were prepared in the same way as MRS agar plates, except that CDMG medium containing 100 mM MOPS was mixed with 1.0% (w/v) agar.

Chromogenic CDMG medium
We prepared chromogenic CDMG medium by adding 1/10,000 (w/v) of the chemical indicator bromocresol purple to the CDMG liquid medium. Chromogenic agar plates were prepared in the same way as MRS agar plates, except that CDMG medium containing 1/10,000 (w/v) bromocresol purple was mixed with 1.0% (w/v) agar. Bromocresol purple was used in the range of 5.2–6.8; greater than 6.8 showed purple color, and less than 5.2 showed yellow color. Therefore, lactate production and diffusion can be determined based on the color change in the medium.

Spent medium generated in agar plates
For Fig. S23A, we prepared spent medium from the agar plate of monoculture A01 by the following steps: (1) after A01 was co-cultured with LM for 30h, the agar block (region b, see Fig. 4B) from A01 colony removal was excavated into 1.5 mL eppendorf (EP) tubes, and the size of the agar block was determined based on the statistical results in Fig. S19; (2) the resources and metabolites were extracted from the agar block, the as shown in the steps of Fig. 4B; (3) as the lactate concentration was close to 100 mM at 30h (see Fig. 4E), the concentration decreased after extraction and we added lactate to the EP tube to bring it up to 100 mM; (4) the above-mixed solution was filtered through a 0.22 µm filter membrane into a 2.0 mL EP tube and recorded as the spent medium.

Spent medium generated in liquid medium
After the monocultures were grown to the target time, the culture solution was filtered through a 0.22 µm filter membrane, and the filtered solution was recorded as the spent medium.

100 mM lactate-acidified CDMG or CDMS liquid medium
The lactate was first filtered through a 0.22 µm filter membrane and then added to sterilized CDMG liquid medium until the final concentration of lactate was 100 mM. Since the lactate concentration at 30h was close to 100 mM (see Fig. 4E), the final concentration of lactate for all acidified media was 100 mM, unless otherwise noted, for example, 60 mM in Fig. 4G, 140 mM in Fig. 5B. The preparation of 100 mM lactate-acidified CDMS liquid medium was the same. The glucose content in the acidified CDMG liquid medium is 25 mM, and the sucrose content in the acidified CDMS liquid medium is 20 mM, unless otherwise specified. For example, Fig. S28 contains three concentrations of glucose: 25 mM, 20 mM, and 15 mM.

100 mM lactate-acidified CDMG or CDMS liquid medium supplemented with public goods
Lactate and supplements (containing public goods: pyruvate, glutamate, and aspartate) were first filtered through a 0.22 µm filter membrane, then lactate was added to sterilized CDMG or CDMS medium until the final concentration of lactate was 100 mM, and finally, supplements were added to it until the final concentration. The final concentration of the supplement was determined based on the concentration of the public goods monitored after 27–30h of co-cultivation, as specified in Figs. 4F, 7B, F, and S27. For Figs. 5D, 7C, G, public goods in the medium were added at different concentrations; specific concentrations supplemented are shown in Table S4.

CDMG agar plates supplemented with the inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate
For Figs. 5E, F, and S24, we prepared an inhibitor-added CDMG medium by adding 120 mM inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate to the CDMG liquid medium. The inhibitor-added CDMG agar plates were prepared in the same way as MRS agar plates, except that CDMG medium containing 120 mM inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate was mixed with 1.0% (w/v) agar.

Spent medium generated in CDMG agar plates supplemented with the inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate
For Fig. S25, we prepared spent medium from CDMG agar plates supplemented with the inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate. A spent medium containing 3-bromopyruvic acid was prepared according to the methods of Fig. S23A. To remove the 3-bromopyruvic acid from the spent medium, we utilized Amberlite IRA-400 resin to adsorb the 3-bromopyruvic acid without affecting public goods. The specific steps were as follows: (1) mix the resin with a solution containing 3-bromopyruvic acid and public goods, stirring at 4×g/min for 60 min; (2) centrifuge the above solution at 5152×g/min for 2 min; and (3) collect the supernatant to be recorded as the spent medium.

Plasmids and strains construction
The fluorescent expression plasmids utilized in this study were developed from a lactic acid bacteria-Escherichia coli shuttle vector, pNZ8148, which contains a PnisA promoter, a Cm resistance gene, and an Em resistance gene (Table S3). The fluorescent protein sequence can be found in Supplementary Notes 7–9, and the primer sequences used for fluorescent plasmid construction are shown in Table S3. Gibson assembly was chosen to construct all fluorescent reporter plasmids, such as lcnA-eGFP, which enhances the expression of green fluorescent protein (eGFP) under the regulation of a constitutive promoter from the lcnA gene. Similarly, plasmids lcnA-mCherry and lcnA-YFP were constructed using mCherry and YFP, respectively, instead of eGFP, to allow for the constitutive expression of these fluorescent proteins.

The LAB was first purified by streaking onto an MRS agar plate and cultured overnight at 37°C. The monoclonal was inoculated into 2 mL fresh MRS medium and cultured at 37°C for 24h. 2 mL of culture was extracted with genomic DNA via a bacterial genomic DNA extraction kit. The extracted genome was used as a template to amplify the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) gene by PCR primers (pGhostΔldh-F and pGhostΔldh-R). The amplified fragments were spliced using overlapping PCR and ligated to the pMD19T cloning vector, and then transformed into competent cells of E. coli DH5α receptor cells for positive clone screening. E. coli X-L-blue containing the pGhost4 plasmid was inoculated with LB medium containing erythromycin at 30°C for 12–16h to extract the pGhost4 plasmid. Subsequently, it was used for the construction of recombinant knockout plasmids. The construction system and reactions were as follows: 3 µL pGhost4, 4 µL splice fragment, 1 µL T4 ligase, and 2 µL 10× loading buffer. The recombinant knockout plasmids were transformed into competent E. coli X-L-Blue cells and coated with LB plates containing erythromycin. Positive validation of recombinant knockout plasmids was performed after overnight culture at 30°C. 10 µL of successful recombinant knockout plasmid was added to 100 µL of competent cells of LAB, then mixed and added to a 0.2 mm electroshock cup for electrotransfection. The electrotransfection conditions were as follows: 2500 V, 200 Ω, 25 µF, and 5 ms. 500 µL of recovery medium was added after electrotransfection, then coated in MRS solid medium containing erythromycin for 24h at 30°C. The monoclonal was picked and incubated in an MRS liquid medium containing erythromycin for 24h at 37°C. The genome was extracted and then amplified using lactate dehydrogenase gene primers and knockout primers, respectively, for positive knockout strain identification.

Culture conditions for microbial strains
All cultures (except for those grown in the plasmids and strains construction, see above) were grown statically at 30°C. Each growth/biomass assay experiment consisted of three steps: (1) seed cultures, (2) pre-cultures, and (3) experimental cultures. Strains stored from −80°C were individually inoculated in CDMG liquid medium to start a seed culture until an OD600 of 0.8 was achieved. This seed culture was inoculated at 1% (v/v) inoculum into fresh CDMG liquid medium and incubated until exponential growth. This pre-culture was re-inoculated at 1% (v/v) inoculum into fresh liquid CDMG medium and this monoculture was sampled for various measurements such as biomass, metabolites, spent medium, etc. Unless otherwise indicated, all liquid media used to prepare cultures had a volume of 2 mL.

Growth of pure culture
Growth of pure culture
The pure culture was defined when only one strain was cultured in the agar plate (Table S1).
For the CDMG solid culture in Fig. 1, three lactic acid bacteria (LAB), LM, LC4, and LC2, preserved in the laboratory, were inoculated in CDMG liquid medium at 1% inoculum (v/v%) for overnight culture, respectively. The overnight culture was diluted to an OD600 of 0.2–0.3, and each of the three LAB was inoculated in the center of CDMG solid medium at an inoculum of 2 µL and incubated at 30°C for 1.5–2 days.
For Figs. S5 and S20, a single strain (LM, B01, or A01) was inoculated in the center of the CDMG agar plate at an inoculum of 2 µL and incubated at 30°C for the corresponding time.
For the CDMS agar plate in Fig. S31A, LM was cultured in CDMS in the same way as in CDMG, except that the sugar added to the medium was different.

Biomass determination of pure culture in agar plates
For Fig. S2, firstly, the individual clones were mined from the agar plates into 1.5 mL EP tubes and rinsed three times using 500 µL of sterile water to obtain bacterial fluid. Subsequently, the bacterial fluid from the three rinses was collected in 2 mL EP tubes and centrifuged at 3578×g/min for 2 min to collect the cells. Next, the cells were resuspended using 500 µL of sterile water. Finally, 200 µL of resuspension was pipetted into a 96-well plate, and the absorbance value was measured by a photometer at 600 nm and recorded as biomass (OD600).

Growth of monoculture
Monoculture in CDMG liquid medium. The monoculture was defined when only one strain was cultured in the liquid medium (Table S1). For the CDMG liquid cultures in Fig. 1B, clones from different locations cultured on CDMG agar plates were inoculated into fresh CDMG medium and diluted to 0.6 of OD600, then inoculated at 1% (v/v%) into fresh CDMG medium and incubated for 16h at 30°C to assay for biomass and lactate production.

Biomass determination of monoculture in liquid medium
After the individual strains were cultured according to the above culture conditions, the monocultures were thoroughly mixed, and 1 mL was removed to a new EP tube. Then, the cells were collected by centrifugation at 3578×g/min for 5 min. The cells were washed three times with 500 µL of sterile water and then resuspended in 500 µL of sterile water. The 200 µL of resuspension was pipetted into a 96-well plate, and the absorbance value was measured by a photometer at 600 nm and recorded as biomass (OD600).

Monoculture in CDMG or CDMS agar plates
The monoculture was defined as inoculations of a single competitor strain at different distances to the right of the producer LM, with different distances being inoculated on separate agar plates. The producer LM and one other competitor were cultured overnight in CDMG or CDMS liquid medium. According to Fig. 1B, lactate started to diffuse at 10h. Unless otherwise stated, producer LM was inoculated for growth for 10h before inoculation with another competitor. A 2 µL (OD600=0.2–0.3) of competitor was drop-plated at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, and 4.5 cm to the right of the producer LM, and the growth of the competitor at different locations in different incubation times was monitored. For the inhibitor addition experiments, the steps were the same except for the addition of 120 mM 3-bromopyruvate.

Biomass determination of monoculture in agar plates
The biomass of monocultures on agar plates was determined in the same way as that of pure cultures.

Measurement of lactate-dependence of growth rate
For Fig. S12, A01, B01, and EH1 strains were inoculated in CDMG liquid medium containing 20–140 mM lactate and incubated for 24h to detect biomass. Growth rate = biomass/time.

Growth in spent medium
Strains were pre-incubated at 2.5 cm to the right of the producer LM in CDMG or CDMS agar plates for 30h. The colonies were then transferred to 1.5 mL EP tubes, and cells were collected following the steps in Fig. S2. To grow faster in the spent medium, we increased the inoculum amount inoculated into the spent medium (2 mL) to a final OD600 of 0.32 and incubated statically at 30°C. Every 1h interval, 50 µL of culture (well-mixed culture) was pipetted into a 96-well plate, and biomass (OD600) was measured. The value of biomass (OD600) was expressed as the assay value minus 0.32.

Growth in 100 lactate-acidified CDMG or CDMS liquid medium
The strains were cultured in CDMG or CDMS medium to an OD600 of 0.6–0.8, inoculated at 1% inoculum (v/v%) into CDMG or CDMS medium containing 100 mM lactate, and the biomass was monitored at different times. The final concentration of inoculation was an OD of 0.32. The value of biomass (OD600) was expressed as the assay value minus 0.32.

Growth in 100 mM lactate-acidified CDMG or CDMS liquid medium supplemented with public goods
The strains were pre-incubated at 2.5 cm to the right of the producer LM in CDMG or CDMS agar plates for 30h. Colonies were then transferred to 1.5 mL EP tubes and inoculated in an acidified CDMG liquid medium containing 25.0 mM glucose with the addition of supplements (pyruvate, aspartate, and glutamate). The final concentration of inoculation was an OD of 0.32. The value of biomass (OD600) was expressed as the assay value minus 0.32. For S28, the concentration of glucose in the medium was 25 mM, 20 mM, and 15 mM to verify that A01 was able to utilize public goods.

Spatial-temporal diffusion of lactate in CDMG agar plates
For in vitro lactate diffusion in agar plates: lactate was first drop-plated in the center of the chromogenic agar plate at 2 µL per drop until the final lactate level was 194 mM, a concentration that is the maximum production concentration of producer LM in CDMG liquid medium. After drop-plating, the plates were allowed to stand at 30°C, and the lactate diffusion distance was recorded every 3h through a straight edge and repeated three times for each plate.
Diffusion of lactate produced by producer LM in agar plates: 2 µL of producer LM (OD600=0.2–0.3) was drop-plated in the center of the chromogenic CDMG agar plates. After drop-plating, the plates were placed at 30°C for resting incubation, and the lactate diffusion distance was recorded once at different intervals through a straight edge and repeated three times for each plate.

Construction of fluorescence intensity versus biomass (CFU/mL) transformation curves
Firstly, an individual strain containing fluorescent protein was cultured on agar plates. Subsequently, clones with different growth periods were extracted from the agar plates into 1.5 mL EP tubes and rinsed three times with 500 µL of sterile water to obtain the cell solution. Next, the cell solution from the three rinses was collected in 2 mL EP tubes and centrifuged at 2290×g/min for 2 min to collect the cells. Finally, the cells were resuspended with 500 µL of sterile water, and dilutions were performed until the final dilutions had an OD600 between 0.2 and 0.8. The above dilutions with different growth periods were coated, and the biomass (CFU/mL) of the solution was calculated based on the principle that the colony counts were in the range of 30-300. Simultaneously, the fluorescence intensity of the dilutions was measured using a fluorescence photometer. The biomass and fluorescence intensity of different growth periods were fitted to construct the relationship equation (relationship curve). Different strains carried different fluorescent proteins, and the same steps were used to construct the relationship equation. Based on this relationship equation, in ternary and quaternary microbial consortia, the biomass of the corresponding strain can be calculated by measuring the fluorescence intensity of fluorescent proteins carried by different strains. The relationship curve is shown in Table S6.

Determination of biomass when different strains are present in a clone
When a single clone contains different strains, such as ternary and quaternary interactions, the method of quantifying biomass by OD600 is not applicable. Therefore, biomass (CFU/mL) was calculated by measuring fluorescence intensity. The details are as follows: the colonies in the agar plates at different distances were transferred separately to the gradient dilution solution until the OD600 of the final mixed colonies was between 0.2 and 0.8. The fluorescence intensity of the dilutions was measured using a fluorescence photometer in different fluorescence channels, such as yellow fluorescence (YFP), green fluorescence (eGFP), or red fluorescence (mCherry). The fluorescence intensity of different strains can be obtained because the strains carry different fluorescent proteins. Based on the above relationship equation between fluorescence intensity and biomass, the biomass of different strains in mixed cultures can be calculated.

Interaction experiments at coexistence distances
Ternary and quaternary interaction experiments revealed that microbial consortia coexisted near a fixed distance of 2.5 cm. In the later time-series interaction experiments and metabolite detection experiments exploring this distance, the steps were the same as in the interaction experiments, except that the inoculation distance was fixed at 2.5 cm.

Growth of gut cocultures
Binary and ternary interactions of producer LM with gut strains (LJ9, SY2-7, LJ9, and SX131) occurred at a fixed distance of 2.5 cm in the same steps as described above, except that the sample sources differed.

Intracellular metabolites
The intracellular metabolites in the culture were obtained according to the method of Ikeda et al.71 with some modifications. The cultures were centrifuged at 3578×g/min for 5 min, and the cells and spent medium were collected separately. The cells were resuspended and diluted to an OD600 of 0.4, and 200 µL of the diluent, 600 µL of methanol, and 30 µL of a-aminoadipate (50 µM, internal standard) were mixed into a 2.0 mL EP tube. It was immediately frozen in dry ice for 10s, then stored at −80°C. Replace the dilution with 200 µL of spent medium and follow the same procedure. The two frozen samples were concentrated and dried in a vacuum dryer for 15h. The resulting precipitate was resuspended in 150 µL of sterile water. After ultrasonication and centrifugation at 53578×g/min for 10 min, the supernatant was collected for HPLC detection.

Detection of resources and metabolites
HPLC detection of resources and lactates. Resource depletion and lactate excretion in the medium were quantified by HPLC. The colonies were first transferred to 1.5 mL EP tubes, and cells were collected following the steps in Fig. S2. Subsequently, the agar plate where the competitor was located was divided into three regions, a, b, and c (see Fig. S18). Agar blocks from regions a, b, and c (volumes of 108±5 mL, 240 mL±8 mL, and 418 mL±13 mL for a, b, and c, respectively; volumes were converted according to 1 mg = 1 mL) were transferred to 1.5 mL EP tubes and extracted with an equal volume of 5 mM dilute sulfuric acid for 10 min in ultrasound for a total of three times. The extracts were frozen at −80°C and then dried and concentrated in a vacuum desiccator for at least 3 days. Subsequently, the residue was redissolved in 10 mL of 5 mM dilute sulfuric acid. Before high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis, the above-dissolved extracts were diluted to the same volume as the original volume of the agar block in regions a-c, respectively, for normalization. HPLC detection of the resources and lactate in solution was performed as reported in our previous report36. All measurements were repeated three times.

HPLC detection of amino acids
Amino acids in the agar block were extracted with methanol concerning the above procedure. The amino acids were detected via HPLC outfitted with a Gemini 5mm C18 110Å column and fluorescence detection. Samples were automatically derivatized by o-phthalaldehyde solution before HPLC detection. The separation was carried out using solvent A (9.5% methanol and 0.5% tetrahydrofuran) and solvent B (100% methanol). Gradient elution assay was performed at an injection volume of 20 µL and a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min, with the following procedure: 0 min (0% of B, v/v), 6 min (10% of B, v/v), 22 min (10%, v/v), 23 min (80%, v/v), 36 min (0% of B, v/v). All measurements were repeated three times.

Detection of intracellular ATP content
The intracellular ATP content is measured by the BacTiter-LumiTM Luminescent Microbial Cell Viability Assay Kit (COO52S, Beyotime Biotechnology, China), referring to the manufacturer’s instructions for the assay procedure. The specific steps are as follows: (1) The cultured cells were washed three times with phosphate buffer and diluted to an OD of 0.2–0.3; (2) 100 µL of the above cells solution was added to the wells of a 96-well plate; (3) 100 µL BacTiter-LumiTM assay reagent was added to the wells of a 96-well plate; (4) The 96-well plate was incubated at room temperature (25°C) for 10 min at 2×g/min; (5) The chemiluminescence assay was performed using a microplate reader and the ATP content of the cell samples was calculated from their chemiluminescence readings.

Untargeted metabolic mass spectrometry
The cultures were centrifuged at 2290×g/min for 5 min to collect the supernatant, which was diluted 20-fold with sterile water and then subjected to non-targeted metabolomics using a Agilent 6520 time-of-flight mass spectrometer equipped with an Agilent Poroshell 120 EC-CN column. The mobile phase consisted of 10 mM ammonium acetate (pH 5.9) at a flow rate of 250 µL/min, and 2 µL of sample was injected every 2.5 min. After each 30 injections, the column was washed for 5 min with a buffer containing 40% water (v/v), 30% isopropanol, and 30% acetonitrile. The mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) ranged from 20 to 450. The raw data were processed by China Sangong Bioengineering Co, Ltd, a testing organization, using MATLAB, whereas the compounds were selected from the KEGG and Metlin databases; data are provided in the source data file. The relative intensity of a single metabolite time course was calculated by taking the difference between the intensity of the first time point and the intensity and dividing by the maximum value of that time process. Fig. 5F was plotted based on the relative intensity of the individual metabolite time processes.

Mathematical simulation
Detailed details on the mathematical model can be found in the Supplementary Notes, and the mathematical simulations in Fig. 6 were carried out using Python 3.10.1 or Matlab R2020a.

Statistical analysis
All experiments were repeated at least 2 or 3 times. For more information on replications and statistical analyses for each experiment, see the figure legends and source data. Statistical analysis was performed using XLSTAT 2011.1.04 software (Microsoft, USA) or GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Software, USA), which involved one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test to determine p-values. Figures were generated using the R software (https://cran.r-project.org/), GraphPad Prism 8.0, or Origin 2023 (OriginLab, USA).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The study focuses on the influence of an abiotic stress gradient on the spatial and temporal interactions between microbial partners. The authors demonstrate that the intensity of acid stress can influence the outcome of competition between bacteria occupying similar niches. Furthermore, the study claims that the secretion of metabolic intermediates from one of the interacting partners can support the growth of co-occurring bacteria, potentially promoting mutualism and resilience to acid stress. The authors confirm the generality of the observed patterns by repeating the experiments with bacterial-fungal pairs. I find the research questions addressed in the manuscript to be interesting. However, I did not find any evidence that demonstrates the emergence of cross-feeding in the manuscript. Further, the manuscript lacks clarity in writing with missing details, for example, in the methods section and statistics.
Major Comments:
• For most of the range-based assays, the bacterial communities were spotted at different locations on the same agar plate. Has it been verified that the presence of communities closer to the centre does not influence the stress gradient experienced by the communities farther from the center? It would be better to have the spots at different distances on separate plates. The current experimental design may suffer from the possibility that neighboring colonies at varying distances from the center of the plate could affect each other’s biology.
• For all microscopy images, it is essential for the authors to report each fluorescence channel separately, rather than providing only combined images.
• In the Materials and Methods section, more details are needed. For example, how much media was used to perform the experiments etc.
• General colony competition is normal. In this case, the authors demonstrate that one mechanism involves lactate-based growth suppression. However, this seems like a passive interaction, as the producer does not increase lactate production in the presence of a competitor.
• Certain sections need rewriting for clarity. For example, in the legend for Figure 2c, it is impossible to determine which competitor is present at each location on the plate. Using typed labels would be more effective than relying solely on the original handwritten labels.
• It is unclear how many replicates were performed for each experiment. In some cases, error bars are used, indicating the number of replicates, but in others, error bars are not shown. Is this because the errors are too small to be visible? For example, Figures 3e and 2d do not seem to include error bars. Upon further reading, it appears that the authors have not specified the number of replicates performed, making it difficult to interpret the presented data. This issue is further compounded by the lack of clarity regarding the specific statistical analyses used to support their claims. In the statistics section, the authors mention reporting standard deviation (SD) and using one-way ANOVA to calculate p-values, but this information is too generic, and one-way ANOVA may not be appropriate for all the analyses presented. The statistics section also refers to “box plot analysis and other figures…” (line 1121). It is unclear which box plot analyses the authors are referring to. Overall, the manuscript seems to suffer from limited application of statistical approaches to support the conclusions drawn.
• Isn’t the observation of stable coexistence of both interacting partners at around 2.5 cm a possible explanation for the lactate-based growth rate changes among the two species being the responsible factor? I am not sure why the authors decided to look for evidence of cross-feeding.Even in that case, authors need to demonstrate colony counts for both partners and analyse them relative to pure culture permance to demonstrate cross-feeding
• The authors present fluorescent images of the LM and A01 combinations, but not of the LM and B01 combination. It may be useful to include these, especially since the growth suppression by LM differs for A01 and B01. These results are important to argue that the differences observed are indeed because of some form of interaction between A01 and B0! And not simply an outcome of growth dynamics primarily driven by interaction between LM and the other two focal strains.
• Supplementary Figure S10 shows that the reduction in the growth rate of individual strains (A01, B01, and EH1) in the presence of higher concentrations of lactate captures the phenotypes observed in terms of invasion and coexistence dynamics. Therefore, the role of interactions between partners in maintenance is unclear.
• While the B01 counts might recover due to the availability of pyruvate or glutamate in the environment, this is likely an effect of byproducts and may not constitute mutualistic interaction, as A01 does not benefit from this interaction.
Minor Comments:
• Line 47-49: The sentence is unclear and may need rephrasing.
• Line 137: "Collected at positions"—missing information in the sentence.
• Line 472-473: Is it correct to say that A01 is secreting byproducts to support the regrowth of B01?
• There are grammatical errors in multiple locations throughout the manuscript.
• Spelling mistake: "coating count" in Figure 2e.

### Reviewer 2

Manuscript Title: “Stress-Selected Slower-Growing Species Promote Interspecies Stress-Resistant Mutualism via Cross-Feeding Public Goods: Dynamic Mechanisms of Competitive-to-Cooperative Variation”
Authors: Hui Liao, Liming Wu, Yi Luo, Hussain Asif, Xinlei Huang, Xiaole Xia
Affiliations: Jiangnan University, Tianjin University of Science & Technology
Summary
This manuscript investigates how lactate-induced acid stress influences microbial interactions, emphasizing the transition from competitive to cooperative behaviors within microbial communities. The authors argue that stress-induced heterogeneity selects for slower-growing species, which subsequently enhance mutualism through the cross-feeding of public goods, such as glutamate and pyruvate, thereby promoting coexistence and increasing stress resistance. The study combines experimental approaches, including microbial cultures and metabolomics, with mathematical modeling to elucidate the ecological and physiological mechanisms underpinning stress-induced microbial mutualism.
Upon review, several aspects of the experimental design and interpretation require significant improvement. Specifically, there is insufficient experimental support for some of the claims, incomplete methodological details, and a need for additional testing to validate the conclusions. While the manuscript provides an interesting perspective on microbial ecology, it suffers from conceptual and structural weaknesses that compromise its impact. The research addresses a key question—how microbial communities adapt and shift interactions under environmental stress—but does not adequately support its conclusions and lacks precise definitions for critical terms and mechanisms. Additional experimentation is required to confirm the proposed cross-feeding mechanism and elucidate the underlying metabolic pathways. Overall, the paper shows potential but necessitates substantial revisions to improve precision, scientific rigor, and robustness.
Major Issues:
1. Metabolite Dynamics and Cross-Feeding:
The paper’s central claim revolves around metabolite cross-feeding as a mechanism driving mutualistic coexistence under lactate stress. While the HPLC data provide insight into the presence of key metabolites such as pyruvate, glutamate, and aspartate, they do not fully establish a direct link between these metabolites and their effects on microbial growth. More direct experimentation is required to confirm the proposed cross-feeding mechanism. For instance, supplementation experiments where different concentrations of these metabolites are added to mono-cultures or consortia would allow for a more robust validation of their role in driving mutualism. Additionally, the use of knockouts or inhibitors that block the production of these public goods could help confirm their necessity in the observed cooperative dynamics.
2. Mechanistic Gaps in Discussion:
The study provides evidence of a shift from competition to cooperation between microbial species under lactate stress, driven by metabolite exchange. However, the metabolic mechanisms underlying this shift are not sufficiently explored. While the paper shows that certain metabolites are excreted and cross-fed, the reasons for their secretion and how they influence species growth remain unclear. The mathematical model used to simulate these interactions, while valuable for predicting dynamics, does not provide biological insights into the metabolic pathways involved. Further experiments are needed to investigate the metabolic basis of this cross-feeding. Specifically, detailed time-resolved metabolomics or metabolite supplementation studies could offer deeper insight into how these processes evolve and whether they can be generalized to other microbial systems or stressors.
3. Insufficient Statistical Transparency:
The statistical methods used in the manuscript are not adequately explained. The authors reference differences between experimental groups without detailing key aspects such as the statistical tests performed, the assumptions underlying these tests, sample sizes, or exact p-values. Furthermore, figures and tables should include more information on the number of replicates, statistical significance, and comparisons made between groups. Providing clearer and more comprehensive details on the statistical analyses would improve the transparency and reliability of the conclusions.
4. Overgeneralization of Findings:
While the experimental data on microbial interactions under lactate stress are intriguing, the authors overgeneralize their findings, suggesting that the principles observed in their limited model system can be broadly applied to microbial communities in diverse environments. The study focuses on a small number of species and a single stress condition (lactate), yet the conclusions are extended to suggest general principles for microbial community behavior under stress. The authors should acknowledge the limitations of their system and temper their conclusions, avoiding broad claims that are not supported by the data.
5. Conceptual Ambiguity:
The manuscript lacks clarity on key concepts such as "public goods," "cross-feeding," and "mutualism." Although cross-feeding is often presented as a cooperative interaction, it can also result in competition depending on the context. The authors do not clearly define these terms or explain how these metabolic exchanges lead to cooperation in this particular case. Additionally, the paper assumes that slower-growing species under stress universally secrete public goods without exploring the mechanisms behind this process. A more thorough definition of these terms and a detailed explanation of how and why public goods are produced under stress would help clarify the dynamics being described.
Minor Issues:
1. Abstract and Title:
The abstract is comprehensive but could be more concise, focusing on the study's main findings and implications to avoid overwhelming readers. Similarly, the title could be simplified to better reflect the core findings. Although it captures the study's scope, a shorter, more direct title may be more impactful.
2. Figures and Legends:
The figures, while visually appealing, need more detailed legends to enhance comprehensibility. For instance, Figure 1, which describes the experimental system, lacks sufficient labeling and explanation of key elements, making it challenging for readers to follow the setup and results. I had a particularly difficult time following the figures, which significantly hindered my understanding of the data presented. To address these issues, I have created a detailed set of comments specifically for the figures as the last section of my review. Additionally, improving the use of colors and data representations could increase accessibility, ensuring that each visual element's meaning is clear to all readers. Including error bars and specifying statistical comparisons in figure legends would also improve result interpretation.
3. Terminology and Language:
The manuscript frequently uses technical terms without sufficient explanation. Terms such as "stress heterogeneity," "interspecific mutualism," and "cross-feeding" are critical to the paper but are not clearly defined or contextualized. Introducing a short glossary or, at a minimum, providing explicit definitions of these terms within the text would prevent confusion, particularly for readers who are not specialists in microbial ecology or evolutionary biology.
4. Simplistic Model System:
The authors use a well-controlled agar-based model system to simulate lactate stress. While this allows for precise manipulation and monitoring, it does not fully capture the complexity of natural microbial communities, which often face multiple overlapping stressors and interact with a wider diversity of species. Acknowledging these limitations in the discussion would strengthen the paper. Additionally, discussing how these results might apply to more complex, real-world environments (e.g., soils, gut microbiomes) would enhance the ecological relevance of the findings.
Figures
Figure 1
In Figure 1, a series of Agar Plates labeled A and B display stages from 0 to 18 hours in A and from 0 to 40 hours in B, presumably representing different lactate concentrations over time. However, this distinction is not clearly conveyed. Although the method section is referenced to clarify these differences, the figure should be understandable on its own without requiring cross-reference to the methods section.
The text describing panels A and B is repetitive, reducing clarity. Instead of duplicating the description, it would be more effective to highlight the differences and specific measurements presented. In panel B, a ruler is used to measure colony growth from the center to the edge, showing distances from 1 to 6.5 cm. However, by the 40-hour mark, when the plate is fully colonized, the ruler indicates a total growth of only 4.58 cm, which appears inconsistent. The authors should clarify this discrepancy.
In panel C, there is a noticeable color difference in the first image of the isolated clones, but the source of this variation is not explained. Clarifying the origin of this color would improve the figure's interpretation. The key message becomes clearer in panel E, where clones at the edge have higher growth rates but lower lactate production rates, while the opposite is true for those at the center. This message could be communicated more explicitly for better understanding.
Finally, panel G, which aims to illustrate the morphological characteristics of the modified strain, is unclear about which specific features should be noted. Providing a more detailed description of the key morphological traits would significantly assist in guiding the reader's interpretation.
Figure 2
The ruler presented here extends from 0 to 6.5 cm, which is inconsistent with the length indicated in Figure 1 (5.5 cm).
Additionally, there is an unnecessary repetition in the text structure between panels (F) and (E), which should be revised for greater coherence.
Figure 3
The experiment involves multiple microbial consortia (ternary and quaternary) with varying initial inoculation ratios. The caption outlines the experimental steps, but it would benefit from greater clarity on the specific methodology for calculating biomass from fluorescence intensity, which is referenced but not sufficiently explained. Since the procedure heavily relies on fluorescence intensity measurements, the figure would be more informative if it included a brief summary of the calculations or a reference to the relevant section in the methods where this is explained in detail.
The experiment analyzes microbial growth across spatial distances, specifically mentioning the inflection point (λx) where the fitnesses of strains A01 and B01 equalize. This term could be confusing without a visual marker in the figure clearly identifying the inflection point. Adding visual cues, such as arrows or markers indicating λx or distances where shifts in fitness occur, would help in understanding the findings. Panel A visually represents the hypothesis of resource-metabolite-mediated coexistence, showing lactate diffusion and metabolite exchange between A01 and B01. Panel B provides a flowchart outlining the method used to extract and detect metabolites via HPLC from different areas of the agar plate. The plate is divided into regions a, b, and c, each representing increasing distances from the inoculated colonies. While the methodology is sound, the panel would benefit from clearer labeling to indicate which areas are closer to the producer LM and which are further away, as this spatial differentiation is key to interpreting diffusion and cross-feeding processes. The caption mentions "normalization" of extracts but does not explain how this was performed, which is crucial for understanding the reliability of the measurements.
Panels C-F present quantitative data on cell counts and metabolite concentrations over time. In Panel C, the temporal analysis of A01 and B01 growth is displayed, with the regrowth of B01 highlighted by a grey-shaded area. Adding context regarding the biological significance of this regrowth phase and the conditions triggering it would improve understanding. Panel D depicts HPLC-detected concentrations of glucose and lactate, while Panel E shows levels of pyruvate, glutamate, and aspartate in the co-culture areas. These panels provide detailed insights into how metabolite levels fluctuate over time in response to microbial growth, but the connection between these trends and microbial behaviors (such as regrowth or stasis) could be better illustrated. Panel F investigates B01 cell counts under different conditions, such as lactate stress alone and in the presence of supplemented metabolites. Structurally, the caption is somewhat disorganized. Dividing the caption into subsections for each panel (A, B, C, etc.) and including well-defined legends, axis labels, and direct annotations on the graphs would make the data easier to interpret.
Figure 5
Panel A presents a schematic diagram summarizing the experimental setup used to assess whether B01 can regrow using public goods excreted by A01. Including details about sampling intervals and the rationale behind using 30 hours of pre-incubation would make the schematic more informative.
In Panel B, the optical density (OD) values for B01 monocultures in the acidified medium are displayed, with or without public goods supplementation. The filled and open symbols effectively differentiate conditions, but the baseline OD600 value of 0.32 should be further explained to clarify its relevance.
Panels C and E illustrate changes in metabolite concentrations over time. Explicit labeling of key time points, such as the onset of B01 regrowth, would provide better context. A clearer description of the HPLC analysis, including normalization methods, would also strengthen the findings.
In Panel D, the relationship between A01’s biomass and glucose consumption over time is depicted. More prominent markers indicating significant time points would improve interpretability.
Panel F showcases metabolomics data, presenting relative intensities of various metabolites in the CDMG medium. Including a legend or labels directly on the graph would help clarify which metabolites are most important.

In Panel A, the model integrates multiple parameters, such as glucose and lactate levels, as well as changes in A01’s internal state due to metabolite depletion. The use of multiple arrows and interacting variables makes the visual layout overwhelming. Adding more detailed labels or a clearer explanation of what each arrow and color scheme represents would improve interpretability.
Panel B provides a cartoon representation of the lactate stress-induced cross-feeding mechanism, which effectively communicates the basic concept but could be improved by linking it more explicitly to the variables and processes defined in Panel A.
In Panel C, the growth dynamics of A01 and B01 are presented over time, with color bands indicating different physiological states. Explicit references to the mathematical model components that drive these phases would enhance explanatory power.
The caption accompanying Figure 6 should be more structured, with distinct subsections for each panel and detailed guidance on how components relate to each other.
Figure 7
In Panel A, the growth dynamics of SY2-7 and LJ9 are shown over time when co-cultured on CDMG agar plates. Providing more insight into why a specific distance was chosen for inoculation and how it affects metabolite diffusion would improve clarity.
Panel B presents HPLC-detected concentrations of pyruvate, glutamate, and aspartate in co-culture areas. Explicitly connecting metabolite concentrations with specific biological outcomes would strengthen the interpretation of the data.
Panel C depicts OD values of LJ9 monocultures in acidified medium. Providing more information on why a specific baseline OD value was used as a reference point would help clarify its significance.
Panel D shows changes in concentrations of public goods in LJ9 monocultures over time. A more thorough explanation of time intervals and how metabolites influence growth behavior at specific points would improve comprehension.
Panels E–H mirror the experiments from Panels A–D, but with sucrose as the carbon source instead of glucose. A more direct comparison of the outcomes would highlight any differences in metabolite production or microbial growth.
Improving the visual organization of the figure, adding annotations to show connections between metabolite concentrations and growth phases, and increasing the font size of axis labels would enhance readability.
The caption could be better structured by breaking down explanations for each panel into subsections to make it easier to follow.
Figure 8
Figure 8 provides a schematic illustration of a general model depicting cross-feeding interactions that promote interspecies resistance and mutualistic coexistence under acid stress. While the figure conveys the overall concept effectively, it lacks sufficient detail in terms of the exact chemical reactions and how acid stress impacts these processes. The interactions shown are somewhat abstract, with minimal labeling of key components, making it difficult to discern the specific mechanisms at play. Clearer annotations, particularly for the movement of metabolites and the effects of stress on these interactions, would significantly improve clarity.
The model does not seem to be directly linked to the experimental results presented in the manuscript, which weakens its overall impact. Incorporating references to specific experimental data or findings would help to ground the conceptual model in empirical evidence. Additionally, the layout of the figure could benefit from a more structured visual hierarchy, which would emphasize the cause-and-effect relationships between acid stress, metabolite exchange, and mutualistic growth. Currently, the figure presents these elements in a somewhat flat manner, which does not clearly communicate the progression of these interactions.
Lastly, the caption accompanying this figure is too brief, failing to provide the necessary context or explanation for the processes depicted. Expanding the caption to explain the assumptions of the model and its connection to the study’s results would enhance the figure’s interpretability. Overall, the figure offers a useful conceptual overview but requires more detail and stronger integration with the experimental data to fully support the conclusions of the manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript provides a systematic investigation of how microbial species can achieve coexistence in heterogeneous and stressful environments. The discovery of a metabolic strategy switch under acid stress, which shifts interspecies interactions from competition to cooperation, is novel and potentially significant. This finding, alongside with its underlying mechanisms, offers important insights into the remarkable diversity of gut microbial communities in the intestines.
Question:
One of the highlights of the study is the interaction between the two Lactococcus lactis strains, A01 and B01, which are portrayed as a typical "cooperator" and "cheater" pair. The experiments are well designed and carefully executed to support the hypothesis, and the findings are presented clearly. I would strongly support the publication of this work in Nature Communications.

## Paper

## Abstract

Acid stress is a central environmental factor shaping the structure and function of microbial communities worldwide. However, there is a lack of predictive understanding of how microbial communities respond physiologically and metabolically to acid stress. Here, we find that higher acid stress favors slower-growing species, promoting population growth and coexistence. Our experiments show that acid stress influences the spatial structure of communities, wherein coexistence is ordered over centimeter-length scales and determined by growth-tolerance trade-offs. We find that interspecific interactions are highly dynamic during acid stress changes, with shifts from competition to cooperation, enhancing resilience under high-stress intensities. Slower-growing species may bolster interspecific coexistence through stress-dependent excretion and cross-feeding of public goods. We construct a resource-consumer-based mathematical model to unravel the processes experienced by species in stress-induced coexistence and their distinct physiological states. Finally, our pairwise bacterial-fungal interaction experiments elucidate universalities in stress-induced coexistence between closely related and phylogenetically distant species with complementary phenotypic profiles. Overall, our work provides insights into how acid stress affects physiological and metabolic responses, as well as overall fitness, resilience, and coexistence.

---

## Introduction

Microbial communities are ubiquitous in nature, shaped by intricate interactions among cohabitating species and their environments1–3. Synergistic interactions between different species perform advanced functions that surpass the capabilities of individual species alone4–6, such as food fermentation7,8, pollutant degradation9,10, and element cycling11. Understanding these interactions will help us decode the operating principles that support and sustain the stability and sustainability of microbial communities. Acid stress is a key environmental variable, shaping microbial community composition7,12. However, aside from the direct effects of acid stress itself, scant attention has been paid to how acid stress changes affect microbial dynamics, including colonization, growth, metabolism, and interactions among cohabitating species and their environments1–3. As global acidification intensifies, altering microbial community structure and stability13,14, it is of paramount importance to untangle the physiological and metabolic responses of microbial communities to environmental acidification and to determine whether there are general principles that can be used to explain these changes.

Although the specific effects of acid stress on microbial communities’ physiological and metabolic processes remain unclear, many investigations of culture-independent omics data in recent years can be used to characterize communities affected by acid stress. In the oceans, for example, profound cyclic variations in community structure are associated with seasonal and long-term acidity changes15,16. Variation in acid stress also drives the quality dynamics of microbially fermented foods, as both microbial diversity and metabolic function shift with varying acid stress7,17. Changes in bacterial community structure and function have also been observed in soils subject to acid stress changes12,18, with potentially important implications for biochemical cycling in a globally acidified environment. Moreover, in the animal gut, acid stress changes can lead to alterations in the structure and function of the gut/host microbiome, thereby affecting health and mood19,20. Thus, acid stress significantly influences ecological processes that control community structure and function.

One mechanism by which environmental change affects community structure and function is through regulating the types of interactions between microorganisms (e.g., competition, cooperation, etc.)21,22. These changes can alter the spatial arrangement of species in the community23–26. Importantly, these arrangements are determinants of community-level properties and specific behaviors, such as the metabolic processes of the microbial community, the resistance of the microbial community to invasive strains, its resilience to environmental stresses, and the evolution of microbial interactions27–30. Nevertheless, competitive interactions remain the dominant interaction type observed in studies27–30. Without a broad understanding of the physiological and metabolic responses of species within the community, it is impossible to determine whether species and communities can be favored in the face of environmental change, especially increasing environmental stress. In particular, few reports have specifically examined the effects of acid stress changes on the outcome of cooperation between microbial species. A small number of studies of synthetic communities and mathematical modeling have shown that microbial communities may cooperate and co-exist when enhanced environmental stress causes another species’ decline23,29. However, the universality of these findings is limited without taking into consideration dynamic feedbacks23,30, making it difficult to assess the natural behaviors of microbial communities. Little is known about how acid stress changes affect colonization, growth, metabolism, and interactions of free-living microbial communities and whether increased stress promotes microbial cooperation.

In this study, we investigate how lactate, produced by lactic acid bacteria (LAB), serves as a prevalent, natural acid stressor31,32. We simulate acid stress changes in many environments, ranging from gut and fermented substrates to soil and oceans, by lactate diffusion over time on multi-microwell agar plates, thus constructing dynamic feedbacks involving interactions within and between species, and with the environment. Specifically, this study systematically examines the growth dynamics, interaction, and stress-tolerant mechanisms of free-living co-cultured communities in response to acid stress using physiology, metabolomics, phenotypic analysis, and mathematical modeling. Our results reveal how the ecological outcomes of LAB communities with different growth rates are affected by acid stress changes, demonstrating that species with slower growth rates are favored under increased acid stress. We also explore lactate stress as a significant driver for interaction variability and metabolic excretion, elucidating that cross-feeding public goods promotes interspecies cooperation and coexistence. Finally, we report experimental results on the interactions between LAB and yeast, confirming the generality of this synergistic stress-tolerant mechanism. In summary, our study demonstrates that free-living microbial communities can respond to changing acid stress by altering physiology and metabolism to promote community-level cooperation and stress tolerance.
